## Overview

Tunisians are the citizens and nationals of Tunisia in North Africa. Approximately 12 million residents live in Tunisia, while a Tunisian diaspora has developed particularly in France, Italy and Germany. The vast majority are Arabs and Berbers who adhere to Sunni Islam. They speak Tunisian Arabic and/or Berber languages commonly found in Southern Tunisia; Tunisian Arabic is a set of dialects of Maghrebi Arabic. The population consists chiefly of Arabs, with smaller European and Berber populations, including Berbers mainly located in the Dahar mountains. Tunisian culture reflects Punic, Roman, Arab, Andalusian, Ottoman, Italian and French influences. Its folk-culture record includes distinctive foodways, music, architecture, dress, jasmine customs, the hamsa, the chechia, and the continuing use of Tunisian Arabic.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name the crescent and five-pointed star on the national flag, and the Sign of Tanit on ancient Punic artifacts.

### Clothing & dress

The *chechia* is the national headgear of Tunisia. It is supple and cylindrical, and its current form was imported from Spain by Moors expelled after the capture of Granada in 1492. These migrants established the craft of the chechia in Tunisia, where it became a second homeland. After independence in 1956, the arrival of manufactured goods and customs from Europe meant that wearing the chechia became limited largely to holidays and religious festivals; it is often associated with elderly people.

The sources also describe jasmine as a form of personal adornment. A man wearing jasmine on his left ear indicates that he is single. Offering white jasmine is described as a proof of love, whereas offering odorless winter jasmine is a sign of insolence.

### Architecture

Tunisian architecture is expressed through Roman and Islamic architecture. Kairouan forms an epicenter of an architectural movement connecting buildings and spirituality through the ornamental decoration of religious buildings in the holy city. In Djerba, the fortress of Kef reflects a military and spiritual destiny connected with Sufi influence.

Many fortresses that protected the coast from Byzantine invasions later developed into cities, including Monastir, Sousse and Lamta. The medina of Tunis is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a typical example of Islamic architecture. Settlements between Bizerte and Ghar El Melh, founded by Moors fleeing Andalusia, have a stronger Christian influence. During the French protectorate, Tunisian cities retained a juxtaposition of architectural styles, including eclectic, neo-Mauresque, Art Deco and modernist styles.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They do identify the hamsa as a palm-shaped amulet commonly used in jewelry and wall hangings.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The *hamsa*, also romanized *khamsa*, is a palm-shaped amulet popular in Tunisia and more generally in the Maghreb. It depicts an open right hand and is commonly used in jewelry and wall hangings. The source describes it as a sign of protection and states that it is believed to defend against the evil eye. Its origins have been theorized in relation to Carthage and the Goddess Tanit.

Jasmine also has a specific social symbolism. It is gathered at dawn, and young boys later sell small bouquets to passersby or motorists stopped at intersections.

## Music & performance

Tunisian music has been influenced by old Andalusian songs combined with Turkish, Persian and Greek influences. **Malouf** is a major form of Tunisian classical music. It derives from the reign of the Aghlabids in the 15th century and is a particular type of Andalusian music.

In urban areas, Malouf uses stringed instruments such as the fiddle, oud and Kanun, together with percussion instruments such as the darbuka. In rural areas, it may also be accompanied by the mezoued, gasba and zurna. Since the late 1990s, new patterns of racial and improvised music have changed the musical landscape. Levantine music of Egyptian, Lebanese and Syrian origin attracts much of the population, while western popular music has also succeeded through rock music, hip hop, reggae and jazz.

Named Tunisian musicians include Hedi Habbouba, Saber Rebaï, Dhafer Youssef, Belgacem Bouguenna, Sonia M'barek, Latifa, Salah El Mahdi, Anouar Brahem, Zied Gharsa and Lotfi Bouchnak.

## Dance & theatre

Tunisian dance reflects migration flows across the country’s history. The Phoenicians brought songs and dances whose traces are described as rooted in the region of Tunis. Religious dances were influenced by Sufism and progressively became Andalusian by the end of the 15th century, together with urban music.

Oriental dance arrived later with the Ottomans. In Tunisia, this form emphasizes rhythmic pelvic movement, arms raised horizontally, and feet moving in rhythm while transferring weight between the right and left leg. The *Nuba* is more rooted in popular practice and is linked to dancers and, to a lesser extent, Kerkennah and Djerba. It is structured into several scenes and is often accompanied by acrobatic games involving jars filled with water.

Tunisian theatre has existed for over a century and has hosted or produced figures including Sarah Bernhardt, Pauline Carton, Gérard Philipe and Jean Marais. On 7 November 1962, Habib Bourguiba devoted a speech to theatre as a means of disseminating culture and popular education; 7 November is regarded as the Tunisian National Day of drama.

## Festivals & rituals

 They do document religious festivals as occasions when wearing the chechia remains common. The Carthage Film Festival has taken place since 1966 and gives priority to films from African and Middle-eastern countries; it is described as the oldest film festival on the African continent.

The sources also describe annual celebrations connected with the El Ghriba synagogue on Djerba. The synagogue is considered a pilgrimage site, and its annual celebrations are linked to its historical significance and to the belief that it was constructed with stones from Solomon’s Temple. Djerba is described as having 39 synagogues, with a Jewish community dating back over 2,600 years.

## Foodways

Tunisian cuisine combines Mediterranean cuisine and traditions. Its spicy character is connected in the source with neighboring Mediterranean countries and with the civilizations that ruled Tunisian land, including Romans, Vandals, Byzantines, Arabs, Spanish, Turkish, Italians, French and the native Punics-Berber people.

The main dish served in Tunisia is *Couscous*, made from minuscule grains that are cooked and usually served with meat and vegetables. Tunisian cooking uses olive oil, aniseed, coriander, cumin, caraway, cinnamon, saffron, mint, orange blossom and rose water. The source characterizes Tunisian food as a “sun cuisine” based mainly on olive oil, spices, tomatoes, seafood, a wide range of fish, and meat from rearing, including lamb.

## Oral tradition & literature

 They do identify Tunisian literary figures and describe Tunisian literature as characterized by a critical approach. Tunisian poetry typically favors nonconformity and innovation, with poets such as Aboul-Qacem Echebbi.

Ali Douagi produced more than 150 radio stories, over 500 poems and folk songs, and nearly 15 plays. Other named literary figures include Khraief Bashir, Moncef Ghachem, Mohamed Salah Ben Mrad, Mahmoud Messadi, Abdelwahab Meddeb, Bakri Tahar, Mustapha Tlili, Hélé Béji and Mellah Fawzi. Themes of wandering, exile and heartbreak are described as central to the creative writing of Tunisian authors abroad.

## Language & religion

Tunisian Arabic is a set of dialects of Maghrebi Arabic spoken in Tunisia. Tunisians also speak Berber languages commonly found in Southern Tunisia, and French is widely mastered. In the Tunisian diaspora, daily speech may mix Arabic with French, English or other languages. Tunisian Arabic is closely related to Maltese, which descended from Maghrebi Arabic and Siculo-Arabic.

The vast majority of Tunisians are Sunni Muslims. The majority follow the Maliki school of Sunni Islam, and their mosques are marked by square minarets. The Hanafi school, introduced during Ottoman rule, is still practiced by families of Turkish descent; their mosques have octagonal minarets. Sunnis form the majority of Muslims, followed by non-denominational Muslims and Ibadite Amazighs. Christianity and Judaism are also present. The Church of Carthage was important in the history of Christianity, while Djerba retains a Jewish community and the El Ghriba synagogue.
